Hi, i'm L2 certified. I want to fly an L1400. I'd like a stable rocket that gets the most out of it and lands under 6 m/s. One stage, nothing fancy. Cheers.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the motor is fixed, an L1400 (exact match required). The goal is the highest sensible altitude it can lift a stable single-stage rocket to (open goal). Landing must stay under 6 m/s (maximum). "Stable" means a static margin of at least 1.0 cal, and I will aim near 1.5. One stage only. No wind or rail length is stated, so I assume the 1.5 m rail and 2 m/s wind defaults.
2. Feasibility: an L1400 is an L-class motor, so somewhere in the 5 to 10 kN*s impulse range and heavy — this is a high-power build with a big mount and a large recovery load. Getting the most altitude means the lightest, lowest-drag airframe that still holds the motor and keeps the margin, and a parachute sized for the real descent mass. Before sizing anything I need the motor's actual impulse, thrust, diameter and mass.

2. Feasibility: the L1400-LW returns 2842.9 N*s over a 2.0 s burn, 1422 N average thrust, 54 mm diameter, 0.736 m long and 2.54 kg loaded — huge thrust for its impulse class. The delay list holds only 0 s, so the motor is effectively plugged and the chute has to go out on an apogee (altimeter) event, which is normal for this size. Feasibility is not in doubt: with this much thrust the whole game is keeping mass and frontal area down while holding a stable margin.
3. Size: the smallest practical airframe for a 54 mm mount is about 0.06 m diameter. Rough build: 1.10 m tube, 0.30 m ogive, about 3.5 kg loaded. Thrust-to-weight = 1422 / (3.5 * 9.81) = 41. Rail exit on average thrust: a = (1422 - 3.5 * 9.81) / 3.5 = 396 m/s^2, so v = sqrt(2 * 396 * 1.5) = 34.5 m/s, far over the gate. Ideal delta-v is 2842.9 / 3.5 = 812 m/s, Mach territory before drag losses, so apogee will land in the several-thousand-metre range wherever the simulator puts it. Descent mass is about 3.5 - 1.4 = 2.1 kg; for a 5 m/s sink under Cd 0.8 the canopy needs A = 2 * 2.1 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 1.68 m^2, a diameter of sqrt(4 * 1.68 / 3.1416) = 1.46 m, so a 1.5 m chute.
4. Draft: minimum-diameter style — 0.06 m phenolic tube 1.10 m long, 0.30 m fiberglass ogive, four fiberglass fins at the tail, 1.5 m nylon chute on apogee deploy, L1400-LW plugged. Checking it.

For the club altitude contest: I want it to hit about 1,050 feet. Keep it to a D or below. Winds are typically 5 mph. Thanks.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 1,050 ft = 320 m (approximate, aim within 5%). Motor class at most D (fixed limit). Wind about 5 mph = 2.2 m/s. Not stated: rail length and landing limit, so I assume the 1.5 m club rail and the usual 6 m/s maximum touchdown speed. Single stage, since nothing asks for more.
2. Feasibility: 320 m with no drag needs v = sqrt(2*9.81*320) = 79 m/s at burnout. A small rocket around 60 g loses roughly half its ideal height to drag, so a C-class motor might just reach it and a D is a comfortable ceiling. I need the real impulse and thrust numbers for both before sizing.

2. Feasibility: the C6 gives 8.8 N*s over 1.83 s and the D12 gives 16.8 N*s. Roughly doubling the impulse would take a light D rocket far past 320 m, so the D12 only makes sense if the rocket is heavy. A C6 in a BT-50 airframe is the closer match, and it stays inside the D limit.
3. Size: estimated liftoff mass 0.055 kg with the motor loaded. Thrust-to-weight = 4.8 / (0.055 * 9.81) = 8.9, well above 3. Average acceleration on the rail is about (4.8 - 0.54) / 0.055 = 77 m/s^2, so rail exit is near sqrt(2 * 77 * 1.5) = 15.2 m/s. That is marginal against 15 m/s, but the C6 thrust spike at ignition should push it higher. Descent mass is about 0.055 - 0.011 = 0.044 kg. For a 4 m/s descent with Cd 0.8, the canopy area is 2 * 0.044 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4^2) = 0.055 m^2, which is a diameter of sqrt(4 * 0.055 / 3.1416) = 0.26 m. A 12 in (0.305 m) chute covers that. Burnout comes at about 1.8 s, and a small rocket coasts for several seconds after that, so I'll take the 5 s delay.
4. Draft: 24.9 mm BT-50 body, 0.46 m long, with an ogive nose, three balsa fins and an 18 mm motor mount. Checking it in the simulator, with the stated 2.2 m/s wind.

4. Check: the simulator gives an apogee of 340.1 m against the 320 m goal, which is 6% high and outside the 5% band, so this draft fails the altitude target. Everything else passes: rail exit 26.7 m/s (my 15.2 m/s estimate ignored the ignition spike), thrust-to-weight 10.0, stability 2.97 cal at rail exit, landing 3.9 m/s with the chute out at 6.9 s. Liftoff mass is 0.0491 kg, lighter than my 0.055 kg guess, which explains part of the overshoot.
5. Fix: apogee is about 20 m high, and the motor can't drop a class without falling well short, so I'll add mass. A small rocket loses very roughly 0.7% of apogee for each 1% of added mass. 5 g is 5 / 49.1 = 10% more mass, which should cost about 7% and land near 316 m. I'm adding a 5 g clay nose weight at the top of the body tube. It also moves the CG forward, so the stability margin can only go up. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: with the 5 g weight the simulator gives 334.7 m. That is 4.6% above 320 m, just inside the 5% band, so the altitude target now passes. The other checks also pass: rail exit 25.2 m/s (at least 15), thrust-to-weight 9.0 (at least 3), margin 3.94 cal at rail exit, landing 4.2 m/s (under 6), motor C6 (inside the D limit). The weight did far less than I predicted: 10% more mass cost only (340.1 - 334.7) / 340.1 = 1.6% of apogee.
5. Fix: none needed after this round; every check passed.
6. Uncertainty: it sits near the top of the band, and apogee depends on OpenRocket's drag model and on the real build mass. If the finished rocket comes out lighter than the 0.0541 kg the simulator used, it will fly higher, so weigh it and add clay. Using the slope seen here, each extra 5 g should take off roughly 5 m. Margin is 3.9 cal, which is stable, but expect some weathercocking into a 2.2 m/s wind.

Quick one: Needs to hit about 9,000 feet and come down within 1,500 m of the pad in 8 mph wind. Dual deploy is fine.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 9,000 ft = 9000 * 0.3048 = 2740 m (approximate, aim within 5%). Drift at most 1,500 m from the pad in 8 mph = 8 * 0.44704 = 3.6 m/s wind (maximum, the hard constraint). Touchdown limit not stated, so I assume 6 m/s. Rail not stated, so 1.5 m. Dual deployment is permitted, and at this altitude it is nearly required.
2. Feasibility: why dual deploy matters here — drifting 1,500 m at 3.6 m/s allows 1500 / 3.6 = 417 s of total descent. A single chute landing at 5 m/s from 2,740 m would take 2740 / 5.5 = 498 s, too long. A drogue descent near 25 m/s down to a 300 m main cuts that to roughly a third. For altitude, ballistic speed to 2,740 m is sqrt(2*9.81*2740) = 232 m/s before drag, so this is J to K territory on a 5 to 8 kg airframe. Checking J420R, K535 and K740.

2. Feasibility: the J420R at 651.2 N*s is far too weak for 2,740 m on a dual-deploy build. The K740 returns 1854.6 N*s at 746.9 N average, 54 mm, 1.469 kg loaded, which is the right class; the K535W at 1428.6 N*s is the fallback.
3. Size: airframe about 4 kg plus the motor puts liftoff near 5.5 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 746.9 / (5.5 * 9.81) = 13.8. Rail exit on 1.5 m: a = (746.9 - 54) / 5.5 = 126 m/s^2, so v = sqrt(2 * 126 * 1.5) = 19.4 m/s. Ideal delta-v = 1854.6 / 5.5 = 337 m/s before losses; on a 76 mm body that should top out in the 2,500 to 3,000 m region. Descent mass is about 5.5 - 0.9 = 4.6 kg. Drogue 0.5 m: v = sqrt(2 * 4.6 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 0.196)) = 21.7 m/s down to 300 m. Main 2.2 m at Cd 0.8 gives sqrt(2 * 4.6 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 3.8)) = 4.9 m/s. Drift budget: (2700 - 300) / 22 = 109 s under drogue plus 300 / 5 = 60 s under main, about 170 s total, times 3.6 m/s wind = 612 m of drift, well under 1,500 m.
4. Draft: 76 mm fiberglass airframe, 2.5 m overall. Ogive nose, 0.7 m main bay with a 2.2 m main on a 300 m altitude event and a 0.25 kg avionics bay, 1.5 m booster with a 0.5 m drogue at apogee, 58 mm mount for the K740, four fiberglass fins. Simulating at 3.58 m/s wind.

4. Check: the simulated apogee of 2263.7 m falls short of the 2,740 m goal by 17%, outside the 5% band, so the altitude target fails. Gates pass with room: rail exit 23.8 m/s, thrust-to-weight 17.6, margin 3.26 cal, touchdown 5.4 m/s, drift 448 m against the 1,500 m cap. Liftoff mass returned 4.33 kg, lighter than my 5.5 kg guess, so the miss is drag, not weight.
5. Fix: apogee 2263.7 m vs the ~2,740 m target, a shortfall ratio of 2740 / 2263.7 = 1.21. The lever is frontal area: dropping the body from 76 mm to 66 mm (still clears the 58 mm mount) cuts area by (66 / 76)^2 = 0.75 while the thinner wall holds liftoff near 4.0 kg, and in the drag-limited regime that should land near 2263.7 * (4.0 / 4.33) / 0.75 = 2790 m. Fins and recovery stay the same. Re-simulating.

4. Check: simulated apogee is 2494.9 m, still 9% under the 2,740 m goal and outside the band. Liftoff mass stayed at 4.33 kg — the thicker wall cancelled the tube mass saving — so the diameter cut only bought 2494.9 / 2263.7 = 1.10 in apogee. Gates still pass with room: margin is now 4.12 cal, far more than needed, touchdown 5.4 m/s, drift 452 m.
5. Fix: apogee 2494.9 m needs about 10% more, and the 4.12 cal margin says the fins are oversized and paying for it in drag at Mach 1.09. Cutting fin area by about a third (root 0.18 to 0.14 m, span 0.11 to 0.09 m, tip 0.08 to 0.06 m) should keep margin near 2.5 to 3 cal while removing a chunk of fin drag. That is the only change.

I'm new to rocketry. It should reach at least 2,500 m and be back on the ground in under 4 minutes, so it doesn't drift off the field. Dual deploy is fine. Wind is usually around 2 m/s. Something I can actually build, please.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the rocket has to reach at least 2,500 m and be on the ground in under 4 minutes. That time cap is 4 * 60 = 240 s. Dual deploy is allowed. Wind is about 2 m/s. Rail length, launch angle and landing speed are not given, so I am using a 1.5 m rail, a straight-up launch and a 6 m/s touchdown limit. One stage, built like a normal high-power kit rather than a minimum-diameter experiment.
2. Feasibility: a single parachute cannot hit both the landing limit and the clock. Coming down from 2,500 m at 6 m/s already takes 2500 / 6 = 417 s, before adding the climb, so the flight would blow past 240 s. The drogue has to do most of the descent and the main can only be out for the last few hundred metres. With no drag, burnout speed for 2,500 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 2500) = 221 m/s, and drag will take a big cut, so I want something in the high-J to L range in a 76 mm tube. Pulling the motor data before I commit to one.

2. Feasibility: J800T is 1264.4 N*s, 665.0 N average, 1.9 s, 0.054 m and 1.0859 kg, with only a 0 delay, so it flies plugged and the electronics eject. J350W is 669.2 N*s in 38 mm, too little impulse for a 76 mm build. J90W is 689.4 N*s but only 97.6 N. On a 2.0 kg rocket that is 97.6 / (2.0 * 9.81) = 5.0, and (97.6 - 2.0 * 9.81) / 2.0 = 39.0 m/s^2 leaves the rail at sqrt(2 * 39.0 * 1.5) = 10.8 m/s, under 15 m/s. K550W at 1624.9 N*s is the modest step up if the J comes up short. K700W and the L730 are there if drag eats more than I think. Starting with the J800T, because it is the smallest motor here that can both lift a fiberglass tube and have a chance at 2,500 m.

Quick one: It needs to break 175 m. Low power only, D motors max. Expect about 3 m/s of wind. Thanks!

2. Feasibility: 175 m is modest for low power. A ballistic pass needs v = sqrt(2*9.81*175) = 58.6 m/s at burnout, before drag. A C-class motor on a light airframe should clear it with room, and even a B might work, but since 175 m is a floor I want real impulse numbers for the candidates: B6, C6 and the D ceiling, D12.

2. Feasibility: the C6 returns 8.8 N*s at 4.8 N average, which is the right band. The B6 only offers a 0 s delay in this database, so it cannot eject a chute, and the D12's 24 mm mount and 42.6 g loaded mass overshoot what a floor of 175 m needs. C6-5 it is.
3. Size: airframe about 0.022 kg plus the 0.0231 kg motor puts liftoff near 0.045 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 4.8 / (0.045 * 9.81) = 10.9, well above 3. On the rail a = (4.8 - 0.44) / 0.045 = 96.9 m/s^2, giving v = sqrt(2 * 96.9 * 1.5) = 17.0 m/s at exit, above the 15 m/s minimum. Ideal delta-v = 8.8 / 0.045 = 196 m/s before gravity and drag losses; on a minimum-diameter airframe that should still land a few hundred metres up. Descent mass is about 0.045 - 0.0108 = 0.034 kg. A 0.30 m chute (area 0.0707 m^2) at Cd 0.8 gives v = sqrt(2 * 0.034 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 0.0707)) = 3.1 m/s. Apogee should come near 6 to 8 s, so the 5 s delay is the first guess.

4. Check: the simulated apogee of 428.9 m clears the 175 m floor by more than a factor of two. Rail exit is 29.8 m/s against the 15 m/s minimum, thrust-to-weight is 13.0, and touchdown is 3.9 m/s with the chute out at 6.9 s and 7.4 m/s of deploy speed. One gate fails: stability at rail exit is 0.77 cal against the 1.0 cal minimum. The fins are too small for this short, light airframe; on a 21 mm body each calibre is only 0.021 m, so the margin is short on absolute distance between CG and CP.
5. Fix: margin 0.77 cal vs the 1.0 cal gate. The fix targets the cause: more fin area at the tail moves the CP aft. Root chord 0.05 to 0.06 m, span 0.035 to 0.045 m, tip chord 0.02 to 0.025 m, sweep 0.02 to 0.025 m; roughly 60% more fin area. Nose weight would also work but it would cost apogee and add build mass. Re-simulating the same design with only the fins changed.

4. Check: with the larger fins the simulated stability is 1.11 cal at rail exit and 1.11 cal minimum through the burn, so the 1.0 cal gate now passes, though the margin is thin. Apogee is 400.3 m, still far above the 175 m floor; rail exit 29.3 m/s; thrust-to-weight 12.8; touchdown 4.2 m/s. Deployment fires at 6.9 s, just before the 7.09 s apogee, at 4.6 m/s. Every gate and the stated requirements pass.
5. Fix: none needed after the fin enlargement; every check passed on this run.
6. Uncertainty: 1.11 cal is legal but thin; a heavier build or added paint shifts it, and it could be widened with slightly bigger fins at a small apogee cost.
